headline: He Built a $1.2 Billion Fintech. A Bank Still Rejected His Home Loan.
subheadline: Dhan founder Pravin Jadhav says a top private bank denied his mortgage because founders are classified as 'high-risk' — the same bank that once honoured him as a fintech innovator.
body:
• Pravin Jadhav, CEO of $1.2 billion fintech Raise Financial Services (parent of Dhan), had his home loan rejected by a top private bank for being a startup founder.
  • The same bank had previously felicitated Jadhav as a top fintech innovator — an irony he highlighted on X.
  • Banks classify founders as "high-risk" because their income is irregular and equity-based, and doesn't fit salary-driven credit models.
  • The episode exposes a structural mismatch between India's booming startup ecosystem and banking norms built for salaried professionals.

Pravin Jadhav runs a company that processes millions of stock trades, pulls in over ₹900 crore in annual revenue, and sits on a $1.2 billion valuation. None of that, apparently, is enough to get a home loan.

The founder and CEO of Raise Financial Services — the Mumbai-based parent of stock trading platform Dhan — revealed this week that a top private bank rejected his mortgage application. The reason: he is a founder, and founders fall into what banks classify as a "high-risk" category.

The Post That Struck a Nerve

"Founder's life is hard! My home loan application got rejected by a top private bank — just because I am a founder," Jadhav wrote on X, adding that the very same bank had, not long ago, felicitated him as a top fintech innovator.

"Founder's life is hard! My home loan application got rejected by a top private bank — just because I am a founder."

— Pravin Jadhav, on X

Jadhav did not name the bank. But the absurdity — an institution honouring the person it simultaneously deems too risky to lend to — resonated widely.

Why Banks Say No to Founders

The rejection follows a logic that is simultaneously sound and deeply outdated. Indian banks underwrite home loans against stable, documented monthly income — the kind a salaried employee at TCS generates. Founders don't fit this template. Their compensation is a mix of modest salaries, equity holdings, and reinvested profits. Wealth is illiquid. Tax returns may show a fraction of actual net worth.

Credit scoring models, built for salaried borrowers, struggle with this profile. A founder sitting on equity worth hundreds of crores but drawing a modest monthly salary looks, to an algorithm, like a borderline applicant.

Jadhav is hardly borderline. Raise Financial raised $120 million in a Series B round in October 2025, led by Hornbill Capital with participation from Japan's MUFG and BEENEXT. Dhan serves nearly a million active users. In FY25, Raise posted revenue of approximately ₹900 crore and profit after tax of around ₹425 crore. Before founding Raise in 2021, Jadhav built Paytm Money from scratch into India's largest investment platform.

A Pattern, Not an Anomaly

Across India's startup ecosystem, founders running profitable, well-capitalised businesses routinely face friction with basic retail banking services — home loans, credit cards, even salary account openings. The financial system has embraced startups at the wholesale level — venture debt, co-lending, fintech collaborations — while its retail underwriting remains anchored to a world where employment means a monthly payslip.

The Diaspora Dimension

Indian founders and entrepreneurs abroad face a parallel version of this problem. NRIs returning to India often discover that years of self-employment income earned overseas counts for little in domestic loan applications. In the US and UK, founders with substantial equity but irregular W-2 or PAYE income report similar mortgage struggles, though alternative products like bank statement loans have emerged to fill the gap. India's retail lending market has no comparable bridge.

An Industry Reacts

Jadhav's post drew responses from founders, investors, and banking professionals who recognised the systemic blind spot. The episode won't change bank policy overnight — credit models evolve slowly, and Indian banks remain cautious after years of corporate loan defaults.

But the gap between India's startup ambitions and its banking reality is becoming harder to ignore. The country mints new unicorns quarterly and celebrates founders as national success stories. The same founders, it turns out, can't always get a mortgage. Jadhav built Dhan specifically to modernise how Indians interact with financial markets. The irony that his own interaction with a traditional bank produced this result is not lost on anyone paying attention.
diaspora_angle: Indian founders and NRI entrepreneurs face parallel banking challenges globally — non-salaried income from equity and self-employment doesn't fit traditional mortgage underwriting models in India, the US, or the UK. The gap between startup ecosystem growth and retail banking norms affects the diaspora community directly, as returning NRIs often find their overseas entrepreneurial income counts for little in domestic loan applications.
